chunks: From him, from Safwan, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, who said:

I asked him about currency exchange (al-sarf), so I said to him: 'Indeed, the caravan sometimes hurries and departs, so we are unable to obtain the Damascus dinars and the Basra dirhams, and only the Saburi [local/standard] Damascus and Basra are available.'
He said: 'And what is the caravan?' I said: 'A group of people travel together, gathering to depart; and when they hurry, perhaps they are unable to obtain the Damascus [dinars] and Basra [dirhams].'
So we sent the revenue, and they exchanged one thousand and fifty of it for one thousand from the Damascus and Basra [currencies].'
He said: 'There is no good in this. Why do you not include gold with it due to the increase [in value]?'"
I said to him: 'I buy one thousand dirhams and one dinar for two thousand dirhams.'

key_terms.البَصْرِيَّة: Basra dirham (a specific type of silver coin)
key_terms.الدِّمَشْقِيَّة: Damascus dinar (a specific type of gold coin)
key_terms.الْفِرَار: Escape/fleeing (metaphorically used for moving from haram to halal)
key_terms.بِسَابُور: Saburi (referring to local or standard currency of the region)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on currency exchange (sarf) when standard coins are unavailable and a premium is paid?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* elucidates the principle of *fadl* (excess) in currency exchange, permitting a slight increase in quantity when exchanging different regional currencies (Damascus dinars and Basra dirhams) to avoid the prohibition of *riba al-fadl*. Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) validates this practice by referencing his father, Imam al-Baqir, who famously described moving from the forbidden to the permissible as 'excellent,' highlighting the pragmatic flexibility in Shia jurisprudence regarding commercial transactions. The narration underscores the importance of maintaining the essence of exchange while adapting to practical economic realities, such as the unavailability of standard coinage.
